steps.body: Take MORE than one piece and the top number simply counts them: three pieces of a fourth-cut is **3/4**. A fraction is a count of units — 3/4 is really **1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4**, three copies of the building block stacked up.
Shade the five slices, then read the fraction.

widget.prompt: The pizza has 6 equal slices. Move the top dial to shade the 5 slices you took.

commonFractions.feedback: That shades only the one slice left behind. You took five slices.

widget.lowFeedback: Too little is shaded. Count all 5 slices you took.
widget.highFeedback: Too much is shaded. The pizza has 6 slices, and you took 5.
widget.successFeedback: Five of the 6 equal slices are shaded: 5/6. The picture also shows that 5/6 is more than half.

predict.prompt: You took 5 of the 6 slices. Is your share more than half the pizza?
predict.reveal: Half of six slices is three — five slices sails well past it. Benchmarking against a half reads a fraction before any symbols do.

explanationVariants: The top counts the pieces you're talking about — in 5/6, five taken pieces.
Bottom describes the cutting; top does the counting. Two numbers, two jobs.

widget.prompt: What does the TOP number of 5/6 count?

options.label: The pieces you're taking
options.feedback: Five pieces in your hands — the top is the take-count.

options.label: The pieces the cut made
options.feedback: That's the BOTTOM number's job — the 6 records the cut. The top counts what you take.

options.label: The pieces left over
options.feedback: The leftovers are whatever the top DIDN'T take (here, 1). The top counts the taken ones.

options.label: How big each piece is
options.feedback: Piece size comes from the cut — the bottom number. The top just counts pieces.

steps.body: Read any fraction like a **recipe**: the bottom says how to cut, the top says how many to take. 2/3 = 'cut into 3, take 2.' 7/8 = 'cut into 8, take 7.' The jobs never swap — cut downstairs, take on top.

explanationVariants: 4/6 means four sixth-pieces — the top literally counts them: 1/6, 2/6, 3/6, 4/6.
Read the recipe: cut into 6, take 4 — four pieces, each a sixth.

widget.prompt: You hold 4/6 of a ribbon. How many sixth-pieces are in your hand?

commonErrors.feedback: 6 is the CUT count — how the whole ribbon was divided. Your hand holds what the top counts: four.
24 multiplied the two numbers — but a fraction isn't a times problem. The top already IS the piece count: 4.

widget.fallbackFeedback: The top number counts your pieces directly.

widget.prompt: Sort each picture: does it show 3/4, or not?

items.label: A bar in 4 equal pieces, 3 shaded
items.feedback: Fair fourths, three taken — the honest 3/4.

items.label: A bar in 3 pieces, all shaded
items.feedback: All three of three is 3/3 — a whole bar. 3/4 leaves one fourth unshaded.

items.label: A bar in 4 UNEQUAL pieces, 3 shaded
items.feedback: Unfair cut, no names — without equal pieces, the shading can't be called 3/4 of anything.

items.label: A bar in 8 equal pieces, 3 shaded
items.feedback: Three of EIGHT is 3/8 — right count, wrong cut. The bottom must match the pieces.

widget.missFeedback: Check both numbers against the picture: a fair cut into 4, and exactly 3 taken.
widget.successFeedback: Only the fair four-cut with 3 shaded earns the name — 3/3, unfair cuts, and 3/8 all fail one of the two jobs.

explanationVariants: 3/4 stacks three fourth-units: 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4. The top is the copy count.
Count up in fourths on your fingers: one fourth, two fourths, three fourths — that climb IS 3/4.

options.feedback: Three copies of the fourth-unit, stacked — that's exactly what the 3 on top means.
Those are THIRDS — three of them make a whole (3/3). 3/4 stacks fourth-pieces.
Adding top and bottom mixes the two jobs. The 4 describes the cut; only the 3 counts pieces.
Each 4/4 is a WHOLE — that sum is three entire bars. 3/4 is three quarter-pieces of one.

hints: The tray's cut is 12 — every count in this story is in twelfths.
Carrots and peppers together claim how many cups?
The dip gets whatever the 12 cups have left.
explanationVariants: Carrots + peppers claim 5 + 4 = 9 cups, so the dip holds the remaining 12 − 9 = 3 — that's 3/12 of the tray.
Account for every cup: 5 + 4 + 3 = 12. The three unclaimed cups are the dip's twelfths.

widget.prompt: A veggie tray has 12 equal cups. 5 hold carrots and 4 hold peppers; every other cup holds dip. How many TWELFTHS of the tray hold dip?

commonErrors.feedback: 9 counts the carrot-and-pepper cups — the veggies. The dip lives in the cups they DIDN'T claim.
7 removed only the carrots (12 − 5). The peppers claim cups too — subtract both: 12 − 5 − 4.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Total cups minus carrot cups minus pepper cups.

steps.body: You can build any fraction now.
takeaways: The top counts the pieces you take; a/b = a copies of 1/b.
Read it as a recipe: bottom cuts, top takes.
A picture earns a fraction name only if the cut is fair AND both numbers match it.
steps.teaser: the two numbers are about to get their official names — and one of them can never be zero.

concept.body: Quick rewind. Build fractions **piece by piece**: 2/5 is 1/5 + 1/5 — count it on your fingers in fifths: 'one fifth, two fifths.' The top number is just how high you counted.

explanationVariants: Count in thirds: one third, two thirds — you stopped at two, so the top is 2.

options.feedback: Two copies of the third-unit — stacked, they're 2/3.
Those pieces come from DIFFERENT cuts — a third and a half don't stack into 2/3. Same-cut pieces only.
The numbers have jobs, not values to add — cut into 3, take 2 pieces.
